en: In the sequence of training as described for Hayagrīva, one should practice the collection of words twice; having practiced the latter first and the former thereafter, and likewise the former upon the latter word, thus indeed is the *jaṭā* prescribed.
In a sequence consisting of three steps,
one should practice the middle step without first practicing the preceding one; thus,
by implication, there would be a repetition of the middle step.
One should display a slight bend of the eyebrows to indicate doubt.
Regarding the sequence of movement, the treatise on prosody (*krama-śāstra*) shall be the authority;
regarding the deviation from that sequence, grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is primary.
In the case of a transposition of the stated sequence,
the specific distinction is that the vowels remain unchanged in both types of sequence;
in a fourfold sequence, one proceeds by circling as in a threefold sequence.

One should display the form of the middle word; likewise, one should move the collection of words that undergo modification during the transition, as in the *saṃhitā* and in the case of protracted vowels (*pragṛhya*). 4.
Without the *krama* [recitation], there would be no knowledge of the *saṃhitā*, the words, or the accents; thus, the *krama* serves its purpose.
Furthermore, since the specific accentuation of a word-sandhi is distinguished from other sources, the *jaṭā* [recitation] is the means for expressing that. 5.

In this case, the hair-locks (jaṭā) are both produced and joined together by the very accent of the sequence; here, the rule regarding the non-accentuation of a finite verb after another finite verb does not apply,
for the accents are indeed designated by the accents as they are heard.
"Also in words belonging to the class of vocatives (āmantrita).
Thus ends the first section in the Jaṭāpaṭala. Now begins the second section.
Where the middle vowel is elided in the triple sequence during the reversal,
there should be the inclusion of that [vowel] from all sides; otherwise, if it were not included, there would be no purpose [in the reversal].
Or rather, since the determination of the word-form as *abhijāte* was established at that time,
no sandhi of the particle (*nipāta*) was ever mentioned;
nevertheless, it was observed [as such] previously in the *Jaṭā*.
For all vowels should be pronounced in succession;
there may also be tremolos (*kampāḥ*) arising from the junctions of vowels.
At the end of a half-verse, a single word is observed.
Then, having practiced that and paused, one should move forward; thus, by means of the *ṛc*, there shall be only one manifest word, and then an exchange with the subsequent [word] occurs. 9
The syllable *o* is also seen as a vocative when it is being joined [with a following vowel], yet it does not undergo sandhi before a vowel— except for the letter *a*— in the *jaṭā* arrangement.
The other distinction is that it does not undergo euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*);
furthermore, where there is no sequential order, the *saṃhitā* is followed by the *pada*, then the *krama*, and then again the *vyutkrama* (reverse order), which is the *krama*.
"This supreme mode of matted hair would be beginningless," as is agreed by all.
Thus ends the second section.
The Fundamental Training is completed.
